title: Concurrency: why "at the same time" is usually a lie
story:
Ask when something happened on one machine and the question has an answer. Ask whether it happened before something on another machine and you have assumed a shared clock that does not exist. Every machine has its own oscillator, every oscillator drifts, and there is no privileged now that all of them are reading.

Lamport's response in 1978 was to stop asking about time and ask about causality instead. He examined the concept of one event happening before another and showed that it defines a partial ordering of the events. One event precedes another if information could have flowed from the first to the second — either because they happened in that order on the same machine, or because the first was the sending of a message the second received. He then gave a distributed algorithm for synchronising logical clocks consistent with that ordering, showed how it can be extended to a total order, and finally specialised it to physical clocks with a bound on how far out of synchrony they can become.

The word partial is the substance. Two events connected by a chain of causation can be compared. Two events with no such chain cannot, and the point is not that we lack the means to compare them — it is that there is no fact of the matter to discover. Asking which came first is asking a question the system does not answer.

Total order can be recovered, and the manner of recovery tells you what it is worth. You break ties using an arbitrary total ordering of the processes, and that is Lamport's own description. So the partial order is unique and discovered, while the total order is chosen and conventional. Two implementations can produce different total orders from identical facts and neither is wrong.

For everyday concurrency on one machine, the same conclusion arrives by a shorter route. A single processor running two threads is interleaving them, not running them together; at the same time means the scheduler may cut between any two instructions. With multiple cores they genuinely do overlap, and then the reordering performed by compilers and by the memory system means that what one thread observes of another's writes need not match any order either of them issued. In both cases the practical rule is the same: the only orderings you may rely on are the ones you established by causation — a lock, a message, a barrier — and anything else is an assumption the hardware never agreed to.

problem.name: Happened-before
problem.shape: Events occur on independent machines or threads and something needs to know which came first.
tell: code assumes writes become visible in the order they were issued
an ordering is being inferred from wall-clock time across hosts
the word simultaneously appears in a specification
problem.move: Order by causation rather than by clock. Establish ordering explicitly where you need it — through locks, messages or barriers — and treat events with no causal path between them as genuinely unordered rather than as an ordering you have not measured yet. Where a total order is required, choose the tie-break deliberately and record that it is a convention.
problem.invariant: Happened-before is a partial order: events are comparable only when a causal path connects them, through program order or message passing.
problem.breaks: A partial order leaves genuinely concurrent events incomparable, so any total ordering must be manufactured. The tie-break is arbitrary, which means two correct implementations can order the same events differently and any behaviour that depends on which one you got is a bug waiting for a different deployment.

cost.time: synchronisation is the explicit cost of establishing an ordering that did not otherwise exist
cost.space: a logical clock per process, or a vector of them if the full partial order must be recovered
cost.beats: comparing wall-clock timestamps across machines, which produces an ordering that looks authoritative and is unrelated to causation

worked.problem: What does it mean for two events to happen at the same time on two different machines?
worked.reasoning:
Usually nothing — and that is the answer rather than an evasion.

The phrase presumes a shared clock. Each machine has its own oscillator, each drifts, and synchronising them is itself a distributed problem with a bound on how close you can get rather than a solution that makes them equal. So a timestamp from one machine and a timestamp from another are readings of different instruments, and comparing them tells you about the instruments as much as about the events.

The useful replacement is causality. One event happened before another if information could have flowed from the first to the second: they occurred in that order on the same machine, or the first was the sending of a message that the second received, or there is a chain of such steps. That relation is well defined, needs no clock, and is what the 1978 paper establishes as a partial ordering of events.

Partial is the load-bearing word. Where a causal chain exists, the order is a fact. Where none exists, the events are concurrent — and concurrent does not mean simultaneous, it means unordered. There is no hidden truth about which came first that better instruments would reveal, because the system contains no mechanism that could have made one depend on the other.

A total order is available if you need one, and how you get it is instructive: you break ties with an arbitrary total ordering of the processes. So the partial order is discovered and unique, while the total order is chosen and conventional — two correct implementations can produce different total orders from identical facts. Anything whose correctness depends on which you happened to get is a bug that will surface on a different deployment.

The same conclusion arrives on a single machine by a shorter route. Two threads on one core are interleaved rather than simultaneous, and the scheduler may cut between any two instructions. On several cores they genuinely overlap, and then compiler and memory-system reordering mean what one thread observes of another's writes need not match the order either issued them in.

So the practical rule I would state is that the only orderings you may rely on are the ones you created by causation — a lock, a message, a barrier, a happens-before edge you established deliberately. Everything else is an assumption the hardware never agreed to, and it will hold in testing and fail under load.

problem.practice: Take a system where two services both write timestamped records and work out what you would actually conclude from one record's timestamp preceding another's. Then find a place in your code where ordering matters and identify which lock, message or barrier establishes it — and if you cannot find one, you have found the bug.

beats.broke: Two things appear to happen at once, and the phrase at the same time presumes a shared clock that no collection of independent machines has.
beats.fix: Order events by causality rather than by time — one precedes another only if information could have flowed from the first to the second — which gives a partial order that is genuinely defined.
beats.cost: A partial order leaves unrelated events incomparable, so any total ordering must be manufactured by an arbitrary tie-break rather than discovered.

interview.q: What does it mean for two events to happen at the same time on two different machines?
interview.trap: Reaching for better clock synchronisation. Tighter synchronisation reduces the error bar and does not create the fact — concurrent events are unordered rather than ordered by an amount too small to measure.
